extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy and law; legislators
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and normative rules about laws and governments from an excerpt of Montesquieu's De l'esprit des lois. The page sets out criteria for making and judging laws according to types of government and local circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of laws: droit des gens, droit politique, droit civil
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish three kinds of laws: laws about relations between nations (droit des gens), laws about relations between governors and governed (droit politique), and laws among citizens within a state (droit civil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu explains that once men are in society different sets of laws arise depending on the relation considered: between nations, between rulers and subjects, and among citizens. Treat each category according to its proper object and principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the law of nations (droit des gens)
rubrics_metrics.description: The droit des gens is founded on the principle that nations should do the most good possible in peace and the least possible harm in war, without sacrificing their true interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu derives the rules of war and peace from the underlying aims: war aims at victory, victory at conquest, conquest at conservation. All laws of the law of nations should flow from these principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: La loi, en général, est la raison humaine (laws founded on human reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, law is human reason; political and civil laws are particular applications of human reason to each nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws should be seen as instances where general human reason is applied to particular peoples; legislators should seek the 'spirit of laws' by examining relations and applying reason to local circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of laws to the people and their circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws must be especially appropriate to the people for whom they are made; it is unlikely that the laws of one nation will suit another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the nature and principle of government, physical geography (climate, terrain), size, way of life (farmers, hunters, shepherds), the degree of liberty the constitution can support, religion, inclinations, wealth, population, commerce, manners, customs, origin and object of the law, and the ordering of things the law addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should derive from the nature of the government
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws that apply in a state should follow directly from the nature of that government (republican, monarchical, despotic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu defines the three government types and asserts that the first, fundamental laws follow from that nature; understanding the government's structure is prerequisite to drafting suitable laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of suffrage as a fundamental law (in republics/democracies)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a republic, laws that establish the right of suffrage are fundamental; it is essential to determine how, by whom, to whom and on what matters votes are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixing the franchise and voting procedures is as important in a republic as defining the monarch in a monarchy; these rules shape sovereignty and must be explicitly regulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix the number composing assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential to fix the number of citizens who must compose assemblies so one can know whether the whole people or only a part have spoken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu gives examples (Sparta required 10,000; Rome did not fix a number and that omission was a cause of ruin). Legislatures should have clear quorum/assembly size rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: People must name their ministers/magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: In a republic the people's ministers (magistrates) must be named by the people; ministers are not truly theirs if they are not appointed by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fundamental maxim: legitimacy of magistrates in a republic rests on appointment by the sovereign people (directly or by delegates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a senate/council chosen to inspire trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the people need to be guided by a council or senate whose members are elected so that the people trust them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trustworthy advisory or deliberative body should be selected in a way that secures popular confidence — either elected directly by the people or by a magistrate chosen by the people to make such appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electorate capable of judging public facts but not of managing affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: The people are competent to judge public facts (who fought in wars, who is a diligent judge, who is wealthy) and thus to elect others, but they are generally not fit to conduct affairs themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the people's knowledge of visible facts to guide elections while reserving complex administration to qualified magistrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of the people into classes influences stability
rubrics_metrics.description: How a people is divided into classes for political purposes is a central law; the manner of division has determined the success of great legislators and the longevity of democracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu discusses Servius Tullius and Solon as examples; legislative designers must carefully craft class divisions (by wealth, centuries, etc.) to balance representation and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffrage by lot (sort) is democratic in nature; suffrage by choice is aristocratic
rubrics_metrics.description: Election by lot belongs to the nature of democracy; election by choice belongs to aristocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lot provides a fair hope to all citizens and reduces envy, but is defective and must be corrected through design (see vetting, eligibility, review). Choice concentrates selection and is characteristic of aristocratic systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of selection by lot: presentation, vetting and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: To correct defects of lot elections, regulators limited eligibility to those who presented themselves, required examination by judges, allowed accusations of unworthiness, and required post-term review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solon's reforms at Athens are cited: military offices by choice, senators and judges by lot, with controls such as presentation lists, vetting, judicial examination, and after-term accountability to combine strengths of lot and choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public vs secret ballots: public preferred in democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies, votes should generally be public; secret ballots were cited by Cicero as one of the causes of the Roman republic's fall. In aristocracies or senates, secret voting may be appropriate to prevent intrigues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu argues public voting allows leading citizens to enlighten and restrain the populace; secrecy in senates helps prevent factional bribery and cabals.

rubrics_metrics.name: People alone should make laws in a democracy; senate may have temporary force
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a fundamental democratic law that the people alone make laws, though the senate may legislate temporarily (e.g., Roman senatorial decrees effective for a year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use councils and senates to draft or trial laws, but final legislative authority rests with the sovereign people in a true democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy should not use lot suffrage; avoid senate self-appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocracy, electing by lot is inappropriate; senators must not have the right to appoint their own replacements because that perpetuates abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman example: senators were not self-supplementing; new senators were named by censors. Do not permit bodies to self-perpetuate unchecked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate greatness of power by brevity of duration
rubrics_metrics.description: In any magistracy, large powers should be offset by short duration; many legislators fixed offices at one year; too long is dangerous, too short unnatural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term limits are a structural safeguard against abuse — one year is often used; very short terms may work only in very small republics where other factors permit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best aristocracy: excluded populace small and poor (minimize oppression)
rubrics_metrics.description: An aristocracy is healthiest when the excluded portion of the people is so small and poor that the ruling class has no interest in oppressing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipater's Athens example (exclusion only of those under a modest census) illustrates making aristocracy as close to the people as possible to ensure stability and minimize oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy requires intermediate powers (nobility) and a deposit of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchies are characterized by intermediate, subordinate powers (nobility) through which the prince's sovereign power is channeled; there must also be a deposit of fundamental laws located in corporate bodies rather than the prince's transient council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abolishing intermediate powers risks turning a monarchy into a despotism or a popular state; the deposit of laws should be permanent bodies (estates, corporate bodies) that preserve and recall laws when forgotten, unlike the changeable royal council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy or customs can serve as a check in absence of other deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is no deposit of laws (as in despotisms), religion or venerable customs serve as the repository of permanence that can check arbitrary power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu notes that in despotic states religion or respected customs often fill the role of limiting arbitrary rule; legislators should be mindful of these social institutions' restraining effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of despotism: single will, absence of laws, delegation to vizir
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism results where one man governs by his own will and caprice; such rulers tend to be lazy, ignorant and voluptuous and often delegate all affairs to a vizir, producing little deliberation especially in large empires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs of governance for large empires must beware of creating conditions that delegate all power to a single minister and thus undermine deliberation and good administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles that sustain each government: virtue, moderation, honor
rubrics_metrics.description: Different governments rest on different principles: democracy requires virtue (public spirit), aristocracy requires moderation (self-restraint among nobles), and monarchy does not rest on virtue but is sustained by honor (prejudice of rank and condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu argues that virtue is essential to popular government (without it the republic decays), moderation sustains nobles in aristocracies, and monarchy substitutes honor and institutional structures for virtue; use this to assess the stability of regimes.
